# Importing Survey Data {#sec-import}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
source("chapters/survey/_common.R")
raw_file <- file.path(raw_dir, "LLCP2024.XPT")
if (!file.exists(raw_file)) {
  stop(
    "Cannot find ",
    raw_file,
    ". Run the download chunk in this chapter first (see the Overview)."
  )
}

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  cache.extra = c(cache_context, list(data = tools::md5sum(raw_file)))
)
```
:::


## Overview

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="The task: answer a population question from a national survey"}

The chapters in this part of the book walk through one complete analysis of complex
survey data in R, from downloading a raw file to reporting a multivariable model:

1. importing a large survey file (this chapter);
2. data engineering: stacking survey files and joining a lookup table
   (@sec-engineering);
3. cleaning and recoding with explicit checks (@sec-cleaning);
4. survey-weighted descriptive statistics (@sec-descriptives);
5. multiple imputation (MI) of missing data, with a discussion of survey-design assumptions
   (@sec-imputation);
6. bivariate (crude) survey-weighted regression (@sec-bivariate);
7. multivariable (adjusted) survey-weighted regression, a sensitivity analysis, and
   reporting (@sec-multivariable).

**The question.** Is household income associated with reported diagnosed diabetes among adults in the participating BRFSS jurisdictions? Diabetes
is common, costly, and unequally distributed. Income shapes access to healthy food, safe
places to be active, health care, and the time and resources to manage a chronic
condition. We estimate how the prevalence of diabetes differs across income groups,
before and after accounting for age, sex, and race and ethnicity.

These chapters assume you have worked through @sec-data-preparation, or are comfortable
with `dplyr` verbs and joins, and that you know the basics of regression.

:::

## The Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System

The [Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System](https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/) (BRFSS) is
the largest continuously running health survey in the world. Every year, the Centers for
Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the states interview hundreds of thousands of US
adults by landline and cell phone about their health conditions, health behaviors, and
use of health care. In 2024, 457,670 adults in 49 states, the District of Columbia, Guam,
Puerto Rico, and the US Virgin Islands completed the interview (Tennessee did not collect
enough data to be included).

The target is noninstitutionalized adults aged 18 or older in these participating
jurisdictions. The combined results include the territories and exclude Tennessee;
they are not estimates for all 50 states and DC. See the
[2024 survey overview](https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/annual_data/2024/pdf/Overview_2024-508.pdf).

BRFSS is a **complex survey**:

- **Strata.** Each state's sample is drawn separately within strata (for example, by
  region and by landline or cell phone).
- **Primary sampling units (PSUs).** Within a stratum, phone numbers are sampled. In BRFSS
  each respondent is their own PSU.
- **Weights.** People are sampled with different probabilities and respond at different
  rates. CDC's final weight (`_LLCPWT`) adjusts for selection and nonresponse and makes the weighted sample
  match each state's adult population by age, sex, race and ethnicity, education, and
  other characteristics ("raking").

Every estimate in these chapters uses all three. @sec-descriptives shows what happens
when they are ignored.

## Download the data (run once)

CDC distributes the data as a zipped SAS transport file (`.XPT`), a format that stores a
SAS dataset in a portable way. Allow several gigabytes for the downloads, extracted
files, and analysis outputs; file sizes can change between releases.

Run the chunk below **once**, by hand, from the R console in the book's root folder (it
is not run when the book is rendered). It saves `data/brfss/raw/LLCP2024.XPT`. Raw data,
processed data and caches are excluded from Git.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dir.create("data/brfss/raw", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
zip_file <- "data/brfss/raw/LLCP2024XPT.zip"
options(timeout = 600) # allow 10 minutes on a slow connection
utils::download.file(
  "https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/annual_data/2024/files/LLCP2024XPT.zip",
  destfile = zip_file,
  mode = "wb"
)
# The zip file names its contents "LLCP2024.XPT " (with a trailing space), so rename
# the file.
extracted <- utils::unzip(zip_file, exdir = "data/brfss/raw")
file.rename(extracted, "data/brfss/raw/LLCP2024.XPT")
file.remove(zip_file)
```
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Downloading by hand"}
You can also download the zip file from the
[CDC BRFSS 2024 page](https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/annual_data/annual_2024.html) ("2024
BRFSS Data (SAS Transport Format)"), unzip it, and save the file as
`data/brfss/raw/LLCP2024.XPT`. The same page has the codebook, which lists every
variable, its question, and its codes, and the questionnaire version files used in
@sec-engineering.
:::

## Read only the columns we need

The file has 301 columns. We need 14, so we read only those with `col_select`. This
keeps memory use low and makes reading fast. It does not change the survey design: every
one of the 457,670 respondents is kept, with their weight, stratum, and PSU.

| Role | Variables | Codebook label |
|---|---|---|
| Survey design | `_LLCPWT`, `_STSTR`, `_PSU`, `_STATE` | Final weight, stratum, primary sampling unit, state |
| Outcomes | `DIABETE4`, `GENHLTH`, `MEDCOST1` | Ever told you had diabetes; general health; could not afford a doctor |
| Exposure | `INCOME3` | Annual household income |
| Covariates | `_AGE_G`, `SEXVAR`, `_IMPRACE` | Age in six groups; sex; race and ethnicity |
| Continuous-variable example | `_AGE80` | CDC-imputed age in years, capped at 80 |
| Auxiliary variables | `EDUCA`, `EMPLOY1` | Education; employment (used only to help impute income in @sec-imputation) |

: The 14 variables used in these chapters {#tbl-variables}

Names that start with an underscore are variables CDC calculated. In R they must be
wrapped in backticks, as in `` `_LLCPWT` ``, not in quotation marks.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
brfss <- haven::read_xpt(
  raw_file,
  col_select = c(
    `_LLCPWT`,
    `_STSTR`,
    `_PSU`,
    `_STATE`, # survey design
    DIABETE4,
    GENHLTH,
    MEDCOST1, # outcomes
    INCOME3, # exposure
    `_AGE_G`,
    SEXVAR,
    `_IMPRACE`, # covariates
    `_AGE80`, # continuous-variable descriptive example
    EDUCA,
    EMPLOY1 # auxiliary variables for imputation
  )
)

# Check: all 457,670 respondents and the 14 columns we asked for.
stopifnot(nrow(brfss) == 457670, ncol(brfss) == 14)
dplyr::glimpse(brfss)
```

Every column is numeric, but most answers are category codes, such as 1 for "Yes" and 7
for "Don't know". @sec-cleaning turns those codes into labeled categories and keeps
`_AGE80` as numeric age for the continuous-variable example.

## Save for the next chapter

Quarto runs each chapter of this book in a fresh R session, so each chapter saves what
the next one needs. An `.rds` file stores one R object exactly as it is in memory.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
saveRDS(brfss, file.path(processed_dir, "01-brfss.rds"))
```
:::


## How the code in this part is written

- Functions from add-on packages use their package name, as in `dplyr::mutate()`;
  base R functions such as `readRDS()` are used directly.
- `|>` is R's pipe: `x |> f()` means `f(x)`.
- Lines that start with `# Check:` stop the code with an error if an assumption about the
  data fails. A silent check means the data are as expected.
- `tidylog::` versions of `dplyr` verbs print what each step did (rows dropped, variables
  created, share missing).
